problems.title: Find the target in a sorted array
problems.learningObjective: Binary search halves the search space on every comparison: compute mid, compare, discard one half, repeat.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set lo=0, hi=n-1. While lo<=hi compute mid=(lo+hi)/2. If a[mid]==target stop. If a[mid]<target set lo=mid+1 else set hi=mid-1. If lo>hi the target is absent.

answerFormat.label: Enter the zero-based target index or the target value.

problems.title: Find the maximum / minimum
problems.learningObjective: A single linear scan keeps a running best value; it costs n-1 comparisons and no extra space.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Keep best = a[0]. For i from 1 to n-1, compare a[i] with best and update best when greater. best is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.learningObjective: For each element compute the complement; a hash lookup turns a nested O(n^2) scan into one pass.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: For i from 0 to n-1 compute need = target - a[i]. If need is already in the seen set, the answer is (indexOf(need), i). Otherwise insert a[i] into the set.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Move zeroes to the end
problems.learningObjective: A write pointer plus a read pointer relocates non-zero values in one pass, in O(1) extra space.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Keep write = 0. For read from 0 to n-1, if a[read] != 0 swap a[write] with a[read] (or assign) and increment write. Fill the tail with zeroes.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Bubble Sort
problems.learningObjective: Repeatedly compare adjacent pairs and swap inversions; the largest value bubbles to the end each pass.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: For pass from 0 to n-2, for j from 0 to n-2-pass compare a[j] with a[j+1] and swap when a[j] > a[j+1].

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Selection Sort
problems.learningObjective: Scan the unsorted suffix for the minimum, then swap it into place; exactly n-1 swaps regardless of input.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: For i from 0 to n-2, set min = i. For j from i+1 to n-1, if a[j] < a[min] set min = j. Swap a[i] with a[min].

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.learningObjective: Pushing every opener and popping on each closer makes mismatches obvious at the top of the stack.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: For each token: if it is an opener, push it. If it is a closer, pop and verify the popped opener is its match. At the end the stack must be empty.

answerFormat.label: Enter valid or invalid.

problems.title: Stack push / pop simulation
problems.learningObjective: A stack is LIFO: push adds to the top, pop removes from the top, and underflow is the only failure mode.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: push(x): if size == capacity report full, else place x at top and increment top. pop(): if top < 0 report empty, else return the value at top and decrement top.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Basic queue operations
problems.learningObjective: A queue is FIFO: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front, and front/rear wrap around in a circular buffer.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: enqueue(x): if full report full, else place at rear and advance rear. dequeue(): if empty report empty, else return front and advance front.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Linked list traversal
problems.learningObjective: There is no indexing: reaching position k means following k next pointers from the head.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: current = head. For each step, read current.value, then current = current.next. Stop when current is null.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Reverse a linked list
problems.learningObjective: Swapping prev and next while advancing rewires the list in one pass, then the new head is the old tail.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: prev = null, current = head. While current is not null: next = current.next; current.next = prev; prev = current; current = next. The new head is prev.

answerFormat.label: Enter the resulting head node or value requested by the task.

problems.title: Maximum sum of any window of size k
problems.learningObjective: A fixed-size sliding window reuses the previous sum instead of recomputing it: add the entrant, drop the leaver, track the best.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Sum the first k values. Then slide: add a[read], subtract a[read-k], and keep the largest window sum seen. The best is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Two Sum in a sorted array
problems.learningObjective: Two pointers converge from opposite ends: the pair sum tells you which pointer to move, so each step discards one index.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set left=0, right=n-1. While left<right compare a[left]+a[right] with target: equal stops, smaller moves left right, larger moves right left.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Range sum with a prefix array
problems.learningObjective: One preprocessing pass stores every prefix total, so any range sum is a single subtraction: prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Build prefix[0]=0, prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i]. Answer each query [l,r] as prefix[r+1]-prefix[l].

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Kadane's maximum subarray
problems.learningObjective: At each value decide extend-or-restart: carry the running sum forward only while it stays positive, and remember the best seen.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Keep current=a[0], best=a[0]. For each next value set current=max(value, current+value) and best=max(best, current). best is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Merge overlapping intervals
problems.learningObjective: Sorted by start, overlap is one test: the next start is at or before the running end, so extend the end or emit the interval.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Sort by start. Walk the intervals keeping cur=[s,e]: if next.s<=cur.e set cur.e=max(cur.e,next.e), else emit cur and start next.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Next greater element (monotonic stack)
problems.learningObjective: A decreasing stack resolves each element the moment a larger value arrives: pop everything smaller, then push the current value.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk left to right with a decreasing stack of indices. While the stack top holds a smaller value, pop it and record the current value as its answer. Push the current index.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Search in a rotated sorted array
problems.learningObjective: One half of a rotated array is always sorted: find which half, test whether the target lies inside it, and discard the other half.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: With lo/hi, read mid. If a[mid]==target stop. If the left half is sorted and the target lies in it, search left; if the right half is sorted and holds the target, search right; otherwise search the other half.

answerFormat.label: Enter the zero-based index of the target.

problems.title: Detect a cycle (tortoise and hare)
problems.learningObjective: A fast pointer gains one node per round on a slow pointer, so on a cycle they must eventually meet; on a plain list the fast pointer runs off the end.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Advance slow by one and fast by two each round. If they land on the same node there is a cycle. If fast reaches null there is none.

answerFormat.label: Enter cycle or acyclic.

problems.title: Most frequent value (frequency map)
problems.learningObjective: Counting with a hash map trades space for time: one pass records every frequency, and the largest count is the answer.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk the array incrementing count[value] for each value. Then scan the map and return the value with the largest count.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Valid anagram by counting letters
problems.learningObjective: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every letter count matches: add one string, subtract the other, and require all zeroes.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Count each letter of s, then subtract each letter of t. If every count returns to zero the strings are anagrams.

answerFormat.label: Enter valid or invalid.

problems.title: Valid palindrome (two pointers)
problems.learningObjective: Symmetry is checked from the outside in: compare the outermost unmatched pair, and any mismatch decides the answer.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set left=0, right=n-1. While left<right compare s[left] with s[right]: on mismatch return false, else move both inward. Equal all the way means palindrome.

answerFormat.label: Enter valid or invalid.

problems.title: Binary tree traversals (pre/in/post-order)
problems.learningObjective: Preorder, inorder, and postorder differ only in when the node itself is visited relative to its children — the routes are the same walk.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk the tree recursively: preorder visits node, left, right; inorder visits left, node, right; postorder visits left, right, node. Record each visit.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Validate a binary search tree
problems.learningObjective: A binary tree is a BST exactly when its inorder walk is sorted: one descending adjacent pair anywhere disproves the whole tree.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk the nodes inorder, comparing each value with the previous one. If any value is smaller than its predecessor the tree is not a BST; otherwise it is.

answerFormat.label: Enter valid or invalid.

problems.title: Level-order traversal with a queue
problems.learningObjective: Breadth-first order falls out of a FIFO queue: dequeue a node, visit it, enqueue its children, and levels emerge left to right.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Enqueue the root. While the queue is nonempty, dequeue the front, visit it, then enqueue its left child and right child when they exist.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Search in a binary search tree
problems.learningObjective: The BST invariant decides the direction at every node: smaller goes left, larger goes right, and each step discards a whole subtree.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Start at the root. Compare the target with the node: equal stops, smaller descends to the left child, larger to the right child. Repeat until found.

answerFormat.label: Enter the zero-based index of the target.

problems.title: Kth largest with a size-k min-heap
problems.learningObjective: A min-heap of size k holds exactly the k largest values seen: anything smaller than its minimum is irrelevant, anything larger replaces it.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Heapify the first k values into a min-heap. For each remaining value, if it exceeds the heap minimum, replace the root and sift down. The root is the kth largest.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Number of islands (grid DFS)
problems.learningObjective: One depth-first walk claims exactly one island: every reachable land cell belongs to it, so the next unvisited land starts a new one.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Scan row by row. On an unvisited land cell, flood through its land neighbours and count one island. Water and visited cells are skipped.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Max area of island
problems.learningObjective: Area is just the size of one flood: measure each island as you claim it and keep the largest.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Flood each island exactly as in counting, but record how many cells the flood covered. The largest cover is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Rotting oranges (multi-source BFS)
problems.learningObjective: Breadth-first search from every rotten orange at once measures minutes: each wave rots the neighbours, and unreachable fresh means impossible.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Queue all rotten cells at minute 0. Repeatedly rot their fresh neighbours at the next minute. The last minute with a rotting is the answer, or -1 when fresh cells remain.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Word search (backtracking on a grid)
problems.learningObjective: Backtracking is DFS with an undo: mark the cell, explore, and unmark when the path dies — so every attempt leaves the board as it found it.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Try every cell as a start. Walk letter by letter through unvisited neighbours, marking the path. On a dead end unmark and back up. Finding every letter in order means the word exists.

answerFormat.label: Enter true or false.

problems.title: Connected components (union-find)
problems.learningObjective: Each set keeps one root: find climbs parent pointers to compare sets, and union attaches one root under the other, dropping the component count by one.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Start with every node its own parent. For each edge, find both roots by climbing. Different roots union (one fewer component); equal roots are already connected.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Climbing stairs (Fibonacci DP)
problems.learningObjective: The ways to reach step i reuse smaller answers: step 1 or 2 at a time means ways[i] is the sum of the two previous counts.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1. For each step i from 2 to n, record dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]. dp[n] is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: House robber (take-or-skip DP)
problems.learningObjective: At each house decide take or skip: robbing it adds its money to the best from two doors down, skipping keeps the best so far.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Keep dp[-1]=0, dp[0]=money[0]. For each house i, take=money[i]+dp[i-2] and skip=dp[i-1]; record dp[i]=max(take, skip). The last dp is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Subsets (choose / unchoose)
problems.learningObjective: Every element is a fork: include it and enumerate the rest, then unmark it and enumerate without it — the undo is what makes it backtracking.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk positions in order. At each one, mark include and recurse, then unmark (exclude) and recurse. Each root-to-leaf path is one subset.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Permutations (used-flag backtracking)
problems.learningObjective: Each open position tries every unused value: mark it used, fill the rest, then free it — freeing is what lets the next branch reuse the value.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: At each open position, try every unused value in order: mark it used, recurse, then unmark it. Each full path is one permutation.

answerFormat.label: Enter the result requested in the mission objective.

problems.title: Jump game (greedy reach)
problems.learningObjective: One running number decides everything: the farthest reachable index. A cell beyond it ends the run; otherwise it may extend it.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Track reach=0. For each index i in order, if i is beyond reach the end is unreachable; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i+jumps[i]). Reaching the last index wins.

answerFormat.label: Enter true or false.

problems.title: Single number (XOR accumulation)
problems.learningObjective: XOR cancels pairs: a number XOR itself is zero, so folding the whole array leaves exactly the unpaired value.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Fold an accumulator starting at 0: acc = acc XOR value for each value. Pairs cancel to zero and the survivor is the single number.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Prefix search on a trie
problems.learningObjective: Shared prefixes share nodes: walking the query letter by letter either falls off (no words) or lands where every completion hangs below.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Follow one link per query letter from the root. If a link is missing the prefix matches nothing; otherwise every word-end in the landed subtree is a completion.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Network delay time (Dijkstra)
problems.learningObjective: Dijkstra always settles the closest unsettled node first: its distance is final, so every relaxation from it is trustworthy.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set dist[source]=0 and the rest to infinity. Repeatedly settle the unsettled node with the smallest distance, then relax each outgoing edge (dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u]+w)). The largest settled distance is the delay.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Coin change (fewest coins)
problems.learningObjective: The fewest coins for each amount reuses smaller answers: try every coin, take one plus the best for the remainder, and keep the minimum.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set dp[0]=0. For each amount x from 1 to the target, record dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x-c]) over coins c no larger than x. dp[target] is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Minimum connection cost (Kruskal)
problems.learningObjective: Kruskal takes edges lightest-first and keeps an edge exactly when it joins two different groups: the lightest safe edge is always part of some optimum.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Sort all edges by weight. Walk them in order, finding both roots: different roots union (add the weight to the total), equal roots skip. The total is the minimum connection cost.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Unique paths through obstacles (grid DP)
problems.learningObjective: The ways to reach a cell reuse smaller answers: add the ways from above and from the left — a blocked cell contributes zero.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Set dp[0][0]=1 when the start is open. Walk row by row: a blocked cell records 0, any other cell records the ways from above plus the ways from the left. The finish cell is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Longest common subsequence (grid DP)
problems.learningObjective: A matching pair extends the best of the shorter prefixes by one; a mismatch inherits the better of dropping one side or the other.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk the table row by row. A match records the diagonal plus one; a mismatch compares the cell above with the cell to the left and records the larger. The bottom-right cell is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

problems.title: Edit distance (grid DP)
problems.learningObjective: Turning one string into the other reuses smaller answers: a match copies the diagonal for free, otherwise pay one plus the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or substituting.
problems.canonicalAlgorithm: Walk the table row by row. A match copies the diagonal; a mismatch compares above against left, compares the winner against the diagonal, and records one plus the smallest. The bottom-right cell is the answer.

answerFormat.label: Enter the numeric result requested by the mission.

lessons.title: Arrays and running state
lessons.concept: An array stores ordered values. Many linear scans keep a small running state instead of re-reading earlier values.
lessons.example: For [3,1,7], the running maximum is 3, then 3, then 7.

lessons.title: Sorting by an invariant
lessons.concept: A sorting algorithm progressively establishes order. In insertion sort, the prefix before the current item is already sorted.
lessons.example: Insert 2 into the sorted prefix [1,4]: shift 4 right to obtain [1,2,4].

lessons.title: Stacks: last in, first out
lessons.concept: A stack remembers nested work. The most recent unfinished item is handled first.
lessons.example: For (), push the opening bracket, then pop it when the closing bracket arrives.

lessons.title: Queues: first in, first out
lessons.concept: A queue processes items in arrival order. Breadth-first traversal uses it to explore each level before the next.
lessons.example: Enqueue A, then B. Dequeue returns A before B.
lessons.code:
from collections import deque
queue = deque(["A", "B"])
first = queue.popleft()
queue.append("C")

lessons.title: Binary search on sorted data
lessons.concept: Keep a range containing every possible answer. Each comparison removes a half that cannot contain the target.
lessons.example: Search 7 in [1,3,7,9]: compare 3, then search indices 2 through 3.

lessons.title: Follow links, preserve reachability
lessons.concept: A linked list is a sequence of nodes connected by next pointers. Save the next node before changing a link.
lessons.example: To reverse A → B → null, keep B reachable before changing A.next to null.
lessons.code:
def reverse(head):
    previous = None
    while head is not None:
        following = head.next
        head.next = previous
        previous, head = head, following
    return previous

lessons.title: Hash tables and frequencies
lessons.concept: A hash table maps keys to values. Frequency counts make repeated membership and counting queries efficient on average.

lessons.title: Strings and two pointers
lessons.concept: Strings are ordered character sequences. Two pointers can compare mirrored positions without creating a reversed copy.
lessons.example: For radar, compare r with r, then a with a; the middle needs no pair.

lessons.title: Trees and recursive subproblems
lessons.concept: A binary tree node has up to two children. Traversal order determines when the node is processed relative to its subtrees.
lessons.example: Inorder visits left subtree, root, then right subtree. A valid BST produces sorted values.

lessons.title: Heaps and the smallest candidate
lessons.concept: A min-heap exposes its smallest element. Keeping only k candidates makes kth-largest selection efficient.
lessons.example: For k=2 and [3,1,7], retain [3,7]; its minimum 3 is the second-largest value.

lessons.title: Graphs and visited sets
lessons.concept: A graph connects vertices through edges. A visited set prevents cycles from causing repeated exploration.
lessons.example: In A ↔ B ↔ C, marking A before exploring B prevents returning to A forever.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming
lessons.concept: When subproblems repeat, store their answers. Define what each state means and how smaller states combine.
lessons.example: With 1- or 2-step climbs, ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). There are 3 ways to climb 3 steps.

lessons.title: Choose, explore, undo
lessons.concept: Backtracking explores a decision tree. Undo a choice before exploring its sibling so branches do not share accidental state.
lessons.code:
def subsets(values):
    result = []
    def visit(i, chosen):
        if i == len(values):
            result.append(chosen.copy())
            return
        visit(i + 1, chosen)
        chosen.append(values[i])
        visit(i + 1, chosen)
        chosen.pop()
    visit(0, [])
    return result

lessons.title: Greedy choices need a reason
lessons.concept: A greedy method keeps the best local choice when it can be shown to preserve a possible global solution.
lessons.example: For jump lengths [2,0,1], index 0 reaches index 2, which is already the destination.

lessons.title: Bit operations and XOR
lessons.concept: XOR cancels equal values: x XOR x = 0, and x XOR 0 = x. This helps when every value except one appears twice.
lessons.example: [4,1,4] reduces to 1 because the two 4 values cancel.

lessons.title: Tries share prefixes
lessons.concept: A trie follows one edge per character. A terminal marker distinguishes a complete word from an existing prefix.
lessons.example: The words cat and car share the c → a prefix, then branch.
